subject: Cognitive Science
title: Conceptual Change in Science
description: A short lesson to help you apply Conceptual Change in Science.

hook.text: Pluto was a planet for 76 years. Then in 2006, scientists kicked it out of the category.

buildup.text: Scientific progress often requires redefining categories: what counts as a species, element, or disease.

discovery.text: Thomas Kuhn argued that paradigm shifts are really changes in how scientists categorize phenomena.

twist.text: Before germ theory, diseases were categorized by symptoms. After it, by cause. Same facts, new boxes.

climax.text: When categories change in science, so does what counts as evidence, explanation, and truth.

punchline.text: New science often means new categories.

quiz.question: What did Thomas Kuhn connect to paradigm shifts?
options: Changes in how scientists categorize phenomena

details.summary: Scientific revolutions involve fundamental changes in how concepts are defined and related. The shift from phlogiston to oxygen required restructuring chemistry's conceptual system. Conceptual change in science parallels how children replace naive theories with more sophisticated frameworks.
details.whyItMatters: Conceptual change research explains why correct scientific ideas are hard to teach. Students must restructure existing concepts, not just add new facts.
takeaways: Scientific progress requires restructuring concepts, not just adding data
Prior knowledge can resist new conceptual frameworks
Student misconceptions parallel historical scientific errors

faq.question: Why is conceptual change so difficult?
faq.answer: Existing concepts are embedded in larger theoretical frameworks. Changing one concept requires changing many connected beliefs. Students who believe heavier objects fall faster have an entire naive physics that supports this view. Replacing it means restructuring, not just correcting.

faq.question: How can teaching promote conceptual change?
faq.answer: Creating cognitive conflict by presenting phenomena that contradict existing beliefs is effective. Bridging analogies help students map from familiar to new frameworks. Simply providing correct information is insufficient because old concepts actively resist replacement.
